memory_update.text: Energy theme should be split into demand drivers, grid interconnection, T&D hardware, transformers/switchgear, high-voltage equipment, construction labor, utility procurement, grid software, and nuclear fuel cycle rather than only generation assets.

Highest-scoring physical-grid bottlenecks: large-load interconnection, transmission hardware, utility procurement, transformers, switchgear, high-voltage equipment, and customer approval/certification gates.
Highest-scoring nuclear bottlenecks: uranium conversion, enrichment/HALEU, and advanced fuel fabrication. Conversion may be structurally tight but lacks clean public pure-play exposure.

Low-attention energy bottleneck candidates may sit in mechanical line hardware, dry-type transformers, power quality, coated steel, conduit/cable management, grid-edge software, procurement systems, and specialized electrical construction.
Large-load interconnection policy reforms and regional grid proposals are key catalysts to monitor because they can pull forward transmission, substation, hardware, and construction demand.
Earnings indicators to track: backlog, book-to-bill, lead times, margin durability, capacity expansion, customer audits, named data-center exposure, and utility project conversion.
Need primary-source verification for PLPC order timing, robotic installation adoption, utility customer concentration, backlog, and actual exposure to data-center-driven transmission upgrades.
Need company filings and earnings-call verification for HPS.A data-center revenue exposure, backlog, lead times, capacity additions, and whether power-quality/transformer demand is incremental.
Need primary filings and regulatory documents for LEU, BWXT, HON/ConverDyn, and advanced fuel licensing milestones to separate nuclear fuel-cycle facts from thematic extrapolation.

Need source verification for high-voltage equipment suppliers outside U.S. markets, especially customer audits, HVDC order details, facility expansion schedules, and named data-center project revenue materiality.

summary: Energy theme chain map focused on chokepoints rather than obvious mega-cap leaders. The highest-friction nodes appear to be grid interconnection/transmission hardware, transformer/switchgear/power-quality equipment, high-voltage equipment qualification gates, utility procurement capacity, specialized electrical construction labor, and nuclear fuel-cycle constraints. AI/data-center load growth is a major demand driver, but the investable bottleneck value may hide one or two layers upstream in low-attention suppliers, regulated fuel assets, certification-heavy equipment, and procurement-execution gates.

supply_chain_map.node: AI and hyperscale data-center electricity demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Large compute campuses create new firm-power, interconnection, backup-power, cooling, transformer, switchgear, and utility-planning requirements. This is the visible demand driver, but not necessarily where the scarce value sits.

Data centers and industrial loads above large thresholds can be delayed by interconnection queues, cost-allocation disputes, transmission-planning cycles, and utility approval processes. Faster interconnection rules could pull forward demand for transmission hardware, substations, switchgear, and grid services.

Hardware installed on transmission towers must be procured before line crews arrive. Low-attention suppliers may benefit earlier in the project cycle than EPC contractors. Potential bottleneck value may hide in mechanical components rather than obvious power-generation or utility equities.

Procurement determines whether T&D projects advance or stall before field execution begins. Supplier qualification, lead times, material availability, contract risk, and vendor reliability can become practical constraints even when demand and capital budgets are available.

Transformers are schedule-critical for data centers, industrial electrification, renewables, utilities, microgrids, and power quality. Shortages can delay energization even if construction and compute hardware are ready.

supply_chain_map.node: Switchgear and engineered electrical distribution systems
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Switchgear, control systems, and engineered power-distribution equipment are needed before data centers, utilities, and industrial facilities can safely manage and distribute power. Custom engineering and backlog conversion can create scarcity.

High-density compute, automation, renewables, EV charging, and industrial electrification increase the need for reliable voltage conditioning, harmonics management, and resilient distribution equipment. This node is less visible than generation or GPUs.

Renewable integration, long-distance bulk power transfer, and grid expansion depend on high-voltage reactors, magnetics, and HVDC components. Long qualification cycles, audits, high reliability standards, and limited approved suppliers can make this a certification-gated bottleneck.

supply_chain_map.node: Customer approvals, audits, and certification gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Energy infrastructure equipment often requires utility, EPC, international customer, and safety/regulatory approvals. These gates create switching costs and can be more constraining than headline demand.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty electrical construction labor and fleet capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Transmission, distribution, substations, and data-center electrical infrastructure require specialized crews, project management, and equipment. Labor shortages can delay execution even when equipment is available.

Large-load interconnection and grid expansion require substations, breakers, transformers, protection systems, and distribution upgrades. This layer links generation and transmission plans to actual customer energization.

supply_chain_map.node: Electrical conduit, cable management, strut, fittings, and raceway
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: These are second-order construction inputs for data centers, grid projects, telecom, and industrial facilities. They may be overlooked because they screen as construction products rather than energy or AI infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.node: Coated steel, galvanizing, and infrastructure metal protection
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Transmission towers, substations, solar infrastructure, and data-center construction require durable coated metal components. This is an underfollowed second-order node where demand visibility may lag project announcements.

supply_chain_map.node: Grid software, metering, DERMS, and load forecasting
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Utilities need better visibility, forecasting, power-quality monitoring, demand response, and distributed-energy coordination as large loads and distributed resources stress the grid. Bottleneck value may hide in metering and data platforms rather than physical equipment alone.

supply_chain_map.node: Nuclear generation as firm power for large loads
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Firm low-carbon power is increasingly relevant for data centers and industrial electrification. However, generation assets are highly visible; upstream fuel-cycle and regulated manufacturing constraints may be more interesting bottleneck nodes.
Raw uranium supply can benefit from stronger long-term nuclear demand and fuel-security policy, but it is upstream, commodity-sensitive, and less directly tied to near-term data-center construction.

Conversion may be one of the tightest nuclear fuel-cycle bottlenecks, but direct public-market exposure appears limited. This makes it important for chain mapping even if it is hard to express through a pure-play public company.
Advanced nuclear and SMR deployment depends on enrichment and HALEU availability. This node is policy-driven, regulated, capital-intensive, and potentially supply constrained.

TRISO and other advanced fuel forms require specialized licenses, manufacturing know-how, and regulatory approvals. Public exposure is thin, making this a high-friction but difficult-to-map bottleneck.

supply_chain_map.node: Reference leaders in data-center power and cooling
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Visible leaders anchor demand validation for critical power, thermal management, and digital infrastructure. They should be used as benchmarks, not allowed to dominate the funnel, because market attention may already be high.
